blocks.md: Senior CP reflex: when values are huge but COUNT is small, throw away magnitudes and keep **ranks**. Almost every 'impossible' range problem becomes tractable after compression. The second reflex: when the STL lacks a query (rank? erase-middle?), GNU pb_ds probably ships it.
**Compress values to ranks → build on positions. If STL can't answer it, pb_ds can.**

chain.q: Why does deterministic unordered_map get hacked?
chain.a: Hacks precompute a family of keys where every key lands in one bucket (std::hash(ll) is identity on many libstdc++ builds). Your O(n) per op becomes O(n²). Fix: SplitMixHash with runtime seed — see Foundations L4.

chain.q: When is bitset the right container?
chain.a: Dense boolean universes ≤ ~10⁸ bits: sieve flags, subset-DP reachability ('can I form sum s?'), transitive-closure rounds (bitset-AND gives /64 speedup). Memory math must be stated in your head: bits/8 = bytes.

chain.q: deque vs vector in hot loops?
chain.a: deque's fixed slab indirection loses cache locality and has heavier iterators; default vector, reserve, and only switch for true both-end queues. In CP, deque often replaced by two vectors or ring buffer.
Exists on GCC 64-bit: holds products of two 10¹⁸ numbers (~10³⁶). No cin/cout — write print128 via digit extraction. Use ONLY as intermediate; final answers mod back to ll.

import heapq
lo, hi = [], []                            # max-side negated, min-side
def add(num):
    heapq.heappush(lo, -num)
    heapq.heappush(hi, -heapq.heappop(lo))
    if len(hi) > len(lo):
        heapq.heappush(lo, -heapq.heappop(hi))

items.title: Inversion Count (PBDS route)
items.statement: Count inversions in n ≤ 5×10⁵ using ordered_set; then implement merge-sort version and compare constants.
hints: For each a[i]: inversions ending here = i − order_of_key(a[i]).

solutionCode.label: BIT over compressed ranks (and the merge-sort fallback)
solutionCode.py:
def count_inversions_bit(a: list[int]) -> int:
    """BIT over compressed ranks: O(n log n)."""
    if not a:
        return 0
    rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(a)))}   # 1-indexed
    n = len(rank)
    tree = [0] * (n + 1)

    def add(i):
        while i <= n:
            tree[i] += 1
            i += i & -i

    def query(i):                     # count of inserted ranks <= i
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += tree[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return s

    inv = 0
    for seen, v in enumerate(a):
        r = rank[v]
        inv += seen - query(r)        # already inserted and strictly greater
        add(r)
    return inv


def count_inversions_mergesort(a: list[int]) -> int:
    """Divide-and-conquer fallback: same O(n log n), no rank compression."""
    def sort_count(arr):
        if len(arr) < 2:
            return arr, 0
        mid = len(arr) // 2
        left, il = sort_count(arr[:mid])
        right, ir = sort_count(arr[mid:])
        merged, inv = [], il + ir
        i = j = 0
        while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
            if left[i] <= right[j]:
                merged.append(left[i]); i += 1
            else:
                inv += len(left) - i      # left[i:] all beat right[j]
                merged.append(right[j]); j += 1
        merged += left[i:]
        merged += right[j:]
        return merged, inv
    return sort_count(a)[1]

items.complexity: Both routes O(n log n). BIT has smaller constants and less memory traffic than a policy tree; merge sort allocates scratch buffers but is dependency-free.

followups.q: Why must PBDS use (value, index) pairs rather than bare values?
followups.a: ordered_set is a set, not a multiset — inserting a duplicate value silently does nothing, so repeated values would be undercounted. Stamping the index makes every element unique while preserving value order, since pairs compare on the first component first.

followups.q: Why is `inv += mid - i` the right count in the merge step?
followups.a: The left half is sorted, so when a[i] > a[j], every remaining element from i to mid−1 is also greater than a[j]. That is mid − i inversions discovered in one step, which is what turns the count from O(n²) into O(n log n).

items.title: Running Median of Stream
items.statement: Median after each insert/delete, n ≤ 2×10⁵. Multiset-balanced solution; state invariant sizes exactly.
hints: Delete may come from either half — rebalance after EVERY op.
Alternative: two priority_queues + lazy deletion from Foundations.

solutionCode.label: two balanced halves; multiset in C++, lazy-deletion heaps in Python

items.complexity: O(log n) amortised per insert, erase and median query. Space O(n).

followups.q: State the invariant exactly, and why it is asymmetric.
followups.a: lo.size() == hi.size() (even count, median is the average of the two middles) or lo.size() == hi.size() + 1 (odd count, median is lo's maximum). Letting the extra element live in lo makes the odd case a single lookup with no branching on which half is bigger.

followups.q: Why is `lo.erase(x)` by value a bug in C++?
followups.a: multiset::erase(key) removes *every* copy of that value. Deleting one occurrence of a repeated element would silently drop all of them and corrupt the sizes. You must find() an iterator and erase that — erase(iterator) removes exactly one.

items.title: Distinct Values in Range Queries
items.statement: Count DISTINCT values in [l,r], many queries. Offline sweep + BIT over last-occurrence positions.
hints: Keep BIT marking last position of each compressed value.
Answer = prefix sum at r minus prefix at l−1 of markers.

solutionCode.label: offline sweep by right end, BIT marks last occurrence

items.complexity: O((n + q) log n) — sort the queries once, then one sweep with BIT updates. Space O(n + q).

followups.q: Why mark only the LAST occurrence of each value?
followups.a: A value should contribute exactly 1 to any range containing it. Keeping only the rightmost occurrence marked guarantees that for the current right end r, each distinct value contributes exactly one mark, and that mark lies at the largest index where the value appears — so it is inside [l, r] precisely when the value occurs in that window.

followups.q: Why must the queries be sorted by right end?
followups.a: The BIT state encodes "last occurrence as of index r". It is only valid for one r at a time, and the sweep advances r monotonically. Answering a query with a smaller r after moving past it would read a state that has already been overwritten — hence offline processing.

items.title: Anti-Hash Survival Test
items.statement: Frequency counting on up to 10⁶ values designed against identity hashes. Ship splitmix-seeded map; verify against a locally generated collision bomb.
hints: Seed from chrono clock — different every run.
Test BOTH default and custom maps on bomb input.
Fallback: sort+group runs O(n log n) unhackable.

solutionCode.label: splitmix64 with a clock-derived seed, plus the sortable fallback
solutionCode.py:
import os


def splitmix64(x: int) -> int:
    MASK = (1 << 64) - 1
    x = (x + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & MASK
    x = ((x ^ (x >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9) & MASK
    x = ((x ^ (x >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB) & MASK
    return x ^ (x >> 31)


# CPython hashes small ints to themselves, exactly like libstdc++.
# A per-run seed means no fixed input can be precomputed against it.
_SEED = int.from_bytes(os.urandom(8), "little")


def safe_freq(a: list[int]) -> dict:
    freq = {}
    for x in a:
        k = splitmix64(x + _SEED)
        freq[k] = freq.get(k, 0) + 1
    return freq


def freq_by_sorting(a: list[int]) -> list[tuple]:
    """Unhackable fallback: no hashing at all, O(n log n) guaranteed."""
    out = []
    a = sorted(a)
    i = 0
    while i < len(a):
        j = i
        while j < len(a) and a[j] == a[i]:
            j += 1
        out.append((a[i], j - i))
        i = j
    return out

items.complexity: O(n) average with a good hash. The attack turns unordered_map into O(n²); the sort-and-group fallback is an unhackable O(n log n).

followups.a: libstdc++ hashes integers with the identity function and uses a prime bucket count you can look up. Feeding n multiples of that prime sends every key to bucket 0, turning the chain into a linked list and every operation into O(n) — total O(n²). It is a routine hack on competitive judges.

followups.q: Why does seeding from the clock defeat it?
followups.a: The attacker must fix their input before your program runs. A seed drawn at startup means the key-to-bucket mapping differs on every execution, so no precomputed input can target your buckets. Seeding from a *constant* would not help at all — the value must be unpredictable, not merely unusual.

items.title: K-th Order Statistic Online
items.statement: Interleaved insert/erase/query-kth on a dynamic set, n ≤ 2×10⁵ ops — nth_element unusable (no persistence); use PBDS.
hints: Compare against policy-tree-free alternative (sqrt decomposition) for understanding.

solutionCode.label: PBDS find_by_order, or a Fenwick tree with binary lifting

items.complexity: O(log n) per insert, erase and kth query with binary lifting over the BIT. Space O(value range) after compression.

followups.a: nth_element partially reorders the container to place one element correctly, and gives no structure you can maintain. After any insert or erase the arrangement is invalid, so you would re-run an O(n) partition per query — O(n·q) overall. A policy tree or BIT keeps the order statistic queryable across updates.

followups.q: How does the binary-lifting select work?
followups.a: Walk the BIT from the highest power of two down. At each step, if jumping `step` positions covers fewer than `remaining` elements, take the jump and subtract what it covered. You end one position before the answer, so pos is the 0-indexed rank. It is O(log n) with no inner prefix-sum calls, unlike binary searching on prefix sums which is O(log²n).
